reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2: a crime novel published in 1938 by Heinemann (London) and Doubleday (New York), the tenth Albert Campion novel, between Dancers in Mourning and Traitor's Purse; full plot summary and character list. title: Surfeit of Lampreys (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, both chunks. The article covers the plot, a full character list, the title's allusion to Henry I, and the 1950 London stage adaptation by Owen Howell (citing Lewis 1998, p. 136, and Lachman 2014). It describes a detective novel, the tenth Roderick Alleyn novel, published by the Collins Crime Club and "first published in 1941", and as Death of a Peer in the United States. That date is the London edition: the Ngaio Marsh House bibliography gives Boston 1940 for Death of a Peer. Quotes Bargainnier (1981, p. 98) on Roberta Grey and Routley (1972, p. 149) on the novel; neither book was consulted directly. Used to correct the installment 9 record, whose plot said the family had no obvious motive and implied a family member was the murderer, whose characters included a non-existent "Frieda", and whose form was a genre name.

title: Bibliography of Dame Ngaio Marsh's Published Works
reliability_notes: A selection of Marsh's published work that includes the complete crime novel series, with the place and year of the first US and UK editions of each novel, together with her short fiction, non-fiction, articles and plays (fetched in full). It shows six novels published in Boston or Auckland before London: Death of a Peer (Boston 1940; London 1941 as Surfeit of Lampreys); Death and the Dancing Footman (1941; 1942); Died in the Wool (Auckland 1944; London and Boston 1945); Spinsters in Jeopardy (1953; 1954); Singing in the Shrouds (1958; 1959); and Dead Water (1963; 1964). The installment 9 author record had given the London dates. For Death of a Peer, the date is corroborated by bookseller listings of the Little, Brown first edition of 1940 (search-result extracts only). Lists the 1950 stage version of Surfeit of Lampreys with Owen B. Howell among unpublished plays. Used for the Surfeit of Lampreys record and for the dates, co-author and US titles in Marsh's bibliography.

title: Down and Out in Paris and London (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-2 of 4. Covers the background (Orwell's tramping from 1927, Paris 1928-29, hop-picking in 1931), the publication history ('A Scullion's Diary', the rejections by Cape and by Faber with T. S. The publication date is given as both 22 January 1933 (infobox) and 9 January 1933 (text); the record states only the month. Reviews and letters are quoted at second hand. Used for the new installment 9 record (the book had been listed only in Orwell's bibliography).

reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-1 of 3. Used for the new installment 9 record.

title: Inside the Whale and Other Essays (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, one chunk. A short article: published by Gollancz on 11 March 1940, 1,100 copies, some destroyed by bombing; its contents ('Inside the Whale', 'Charles Dickens', 'Boys' Weeklies'); and the different Penguin collection of 1962 with the same title, a reprint of Selected Essays (1957). Used for the new installment 9 record.

title: Inside the Whale (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2. The article on the title essay: background (Tropic of Cancer, Orwell's dinner with Miller in December 1936), a part-by-part account of the argument, and extracts, including the 'necessary murder' passage. Used for the summary of the title essay in the new installment 9 record.

title: Malcolm Muggeridge (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0, 3 and 4 of 5: the lead, early life and career, Moscow, and the full list of works; chunks 1 and 2 (later career) were not read. Gives birth at Sanderstead, Surrey, death at Hastings, Selwyn College, teaching at Union Christian College (Kingdom of Cochin) and in Egypt, Moscow in 1932, the anonymous famine reports of 25, 27 and 28 March 1933, Picture Palace (completed January 1933, published 1934 but not distributed), and Winter in Moscow (1934), described only in outline. Goodreads lists a novel 'Autumnal Face', which the Wikipedia list omits; it is not recorded until verified.

title: Amos Tutuola (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-2 of 4 (lead, early history, writing, reception, selected bibliography, tributes, further reading); chunk 3 (external links) not read. Gives birth on 20 June 1920 at Wasinmi near Abeokuta, death on 8 June 1997 at Ibadan (hypertension and diabetes), Salvation Army and Anglican Central schools (1934-39), RAF blacksmith 1942-45, marriage to Victoria Alake (1947), storekeeper at the Nigerian Broadcasting Corporation from 1956, the Mbari Club, Ife 1979, Iowa 1983, the papers at the Harry Ransom Center, translations into 11 languages, Queneau's French translation (1953), and quotations from Dylan Thomas, Taban lo Liyong (1975), Omolara Ogundipe-Leslie (1970), O. R. Dathorne and Wole Soyinka (1963). Its selected bibliography lists the eleven books of 1952-1990 including The Wild Hunter (1982). The New York Times review of The Brave African Huntress (2 November 1958) that it cites returned HTTP 403 and was not read.

title: Amos Tutuola (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
reliability_notes: Article revised 4 June 2026, read in full. Born 1920 at Abeokuta, died 8 June 1997 at Ibadan; six years of schooling; working as a blacksmith 'from 1939' (Wikipedia: trained after 1939, practised 1942-45); influenced by D. O. Fagunwa and familiar with The Thousand and One Nights and Pilgrim's Progress from school. One-sentence accounts of The Palm-Wine Drinkard (1952), My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (1954) and Simbi (1955); dates for ten books to 1990 (omits The Wild Hunter); translated into 11 languages; stage and operatic versions by others. Britannica's separate Simbi topic page has only an AI-generated summary and was not used.

title: Amos Tutuola (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Gale's Contemporary Black Biography)
reliability_notes: Contemporary Black Biography entry, read in full (page chunks 0-2 of 7). Draws on Bernth Lindfors's essay in Dictionary of Literary Biography vol. 125 and on Contemporary Authors. Gives birth at Ipose-Ake, Abeokuta (Wikipedia: Wasinmi); coppersmith training and RAF service 1943-45; the Labour Department job; the late-1940s manuscript of The Wild Hunter sent to a London photography-book firm with negatives of drawings of spirits; the United Society for Christian Literature passing The Palm-Wine Drinkard to Faber; Dylan Thomas's Observer review (6 July 1952); plot outlines of The Palm-Wine Drinkard, My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (24 years; quoting Lindfors), Simbi (Lindfors's list of ordeals) and The Witch-Herbalist; Edward Blishen's review (Times Educational Supplement, 26 February 1982); Robert Elliot Fox's tribute; selected writings with publishers; honours (New Orleans 1983, Turin 1985, Pan African Writers Association 1992). Its narrative implies 1980 for The Witch-Herbalist, while its list gives 1981.

title: Amos Tutuola (Encyclopedia.com, compiling the Gale Contextual Encyclopedia of World Literature)
reliability_notes: Gale Contextual Encyclopedia of World Literature entry, read in full (page chunks 2-4 of 7). Gives the Focal Press manuscript, Nigerian hostility to The Palm-Wine Drinkard at the close of the colonial era, translation into fifteen languages (Britannica: eleven), plot outlines of My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (24 years; a 'television-handed goddess'), Simbi (first book with numbered chapters and third-person narration), Feather Woman of the Jungle (ten-night frame like the Arabian Nights), The Witch-Herbalist (the husband's pregnancy), Yoruba Folktales (written for primary schools in standard English) and The Village Witch Doctor ('eighteen stories'; ISFDB lists twelve), plus the Fagunwa, Bunyan and Arabian Nights influences, the folktale hero types, a sample of Yoruba-influenced grammar and V. S. Pritchett's New Statesman praise. Internally inconsistent: it places the television-handed goddess in My Life in the Bush of Ghosts in one paragraph and in The Palm-Wine Drinkard in another.

title: Amos Tutuola (Encyclopedia.com, compiling the Encyclopedia of World Biography)
reliability_notes: Encyclopedia of World Biography entry, read in full (page chunks 4-5 of 7). Dates Simbi 1956 and The Witch Herbalist 1980 (most sources: 1955 and 1981) and lists Pauper, Brawler, Slanderer (1987) among his 'similar romances'; names spirits such as the Smelling-Ghost, the Reverend Devil and the Television-handed Goddess without assigning them to books; records E. K. Ogunmola's 1963 Yoruba folk-opera adaptation of The Palm-Wine Drinkard and its success across Nigeria, and the honours of 1983 and 1985.

title: Tutuola, Amos 1920-1997 (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Gale's Contemporary Literary Criticism)
author_or_editor: Gale editors; essay by Chris Dunton
reliability_notes: Chunks 0 and 8 of 13 read; the rest were not. Chunk 0: introduction, biography (messenger in Lagos from 1948), major works, critical reception (Richard Bauerle's review of The Village Witch Doctor, World Literature Today 65.3, summer 1991, p. 539; Steven M. Tobias on anti-realism; Dunton on the unpublished plays) and principal works (Simbi dated 1956; a 1958 drama titled The Palm-Wine Drinkard; The Wild Hunter classed as short stories, 1982, revised 1989). It gives twenty years in the Bush of Ghosts where others give twenty-four. Some details of Ajaiyi (the witch doctor's trickery) were seen only in a search-engine extract of the same page.

title: The Palm-Wine Drinkard (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunks 0-1 of 2 (complete). title: My Life in the Bush of Ghosts (novel) (Wikipedia)

title: Summary Bibliography: Amos Tutuola (ISFDB)
reliability_notes: Read in full. Birth on 20 June 1920 and death on 8 June 1997; novels 1954-1981; the collections Yoruba Folktales (1986), The Village Witch Doctor & Other Stories (1990) and the posthumous Don't Pay Bad for Bad (2012); excerpts of The Palm-Wine Drinkard; Italian translations (1954); short fiction with years of first appearance from 1952 to 1990. Covers speculative fiction only, and its title pages for the individual stories (with their venues) were not read.

title: Publication: Yoruba Folktales (ISFDB record 411186)
reliability_notes: Ibadan University Press, 1986, first edition, v + 57 pages, ISBN 978-121-186-5, printed on demand; cover by Bayo Ogundele, interior art by Kola Adesokan; contents of seven tales with page numbers. The data is taken from OCLC (WorldCat 16907864) and verified against it in 2024; the book was not seen.

title: Publication: The Village Witch Doctor & Other Stories (ISFDB record 409845)
reliability_notes: Faber and Faber, 1990, 90 pages, ISBN 0-571-14215-X, £3.99 (US $7.95, Canada $8.95); cover by Henry Iles; contents of twelve stories with page numbers, four of them with earlier first-appearance years (1960, 1961, 1969, 1974). The record has no primary verification; the Gale Contextual Encyclopedia says eighteen stories.

title: The Brave African Huntress (Faber and Faber product page)
reliability_notes: Publisher's summary of the 2014 paperback reissue: Adebisi goes to the Jungle of the Pigmies to rescue her four brothers, conquers a giant, serves as a king's barber, endures the pigmies' prison and frees her brothers. Promotional copy, used only for plot outline.

title: Ajaiyi and His Inherited Poverty (Faber and Faber product page)
reliability_notes: Publisher's summary of the 2015 paperback reissue: Ajaiyi, born into poverty, travels through strange lands, meets the Spirit of Fire, is helped by a wizard and a unicorn, and finds the answer close to home. Its author note says T. S. Eliot acquired The Palm-Wine Drinkard for Faber; this was not corroborated and was not used.

title: Feather Woman of the Jungle (Faber and Faber product page)
reliability_notes: Publisher's summary of the 2015 paperback reissue: a Yoruba village gathers on ten nights to hear its chief's adventures, among them the Jungle Witch and her ostrich, the town of the water people and imprisonment by the Goddess of Diamonds. Promotional copy, used only for plot outline.

title: Pauper, Brawler and Slanderer (Faber and Faber product page)
reliability_notes: Publisher's summary of the 2014 ebook reissue: the three title characters are forced on journeys of no return; a ploughing competition for the hand of Popondoro; the brief reign of Pauper and Slanderer in the town of women. Its evaluative phrases were not used. This is the only description of the book's content that was consulted.

title: Heinemann African Writers Series (Wikipedia), section "Bibliography"
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (chunks 0-9 of 10). The table states that it reproduces the bibliography prepared by Nourdin Bejjit (Open University PhD, 2009) and printed in James Currey, Africa Writes Back (Oxford: James Currey, 2008), pp. 301-310; Currey's book and Bejjit's thesis were not consulted. All numbered entries 1-270 were transcribed except no. 65, which the table omits, together with the 97 unnumbered titles of 1985-2003 and the contributors the table names for anthologies, into research/installment_10/lists/heinemann_african_writers_series_1962_2003.csv (641 rows). Defects found in the table: the note to no. 31 (A Man of the People, 'originally published 1959') conflicts with the novel's 1966 first publication; the 1995 entry credited to Lindsey Collen gives the title, link and 1983 Braziller edition of Buchi Emecheta's The Rape of Shavi; misspellings (Sepho Sepamia, Cosmo Peterse, Musaemura Zimuya, Molara Ogunidpe Leslie, 'Echoing Siliences', 'tradedy'); many entries of the 1970s-1990s leave the genre and, for translated books, the source language blank. Used for discovery only, never as verification of a work.

title: Iowa Writers' Workshop (Post45 Data Collective; Program Era Project)
author_or_editor: Nicholas Kelley, Nicole White and Loren Glass
reliability_notes: Peer-reviewed dataset: people (3,115 students and teachers, 1931-2014, with country of origin and library authority identifiers), graduations (3,051 thesis records with year, degree and genre) and 1,228 works by Workshop authors held by HathiTrust. Only graduates with an LCCN, VIAF or Wikidata identifier (published authors) and the HathiTrust works dated 1946-2000 were used, as discovery evidence for American writing outside the prize and bestseller records.

title: George Lamming (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (chunks 0-3 of 4): life, career, the six novels, the list of published works (novels, non-fiction, anthologies edited, uncollected short stories) and awards. Used for the biography and the bibliography. Its birthplace link points to Carrington in the parish of Saint Philip, which conflicts with Britannica and Contemporary Black Biography (near Bridgetown); its ISBN for Coming, Coming Home is the one it also gives for Caribbean Reasonings, so neither ISBN was used.

title: In the Castle of My Skin (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (2 chunks). Publication, the source of the title in Derek Walcott's Epitaph for the Young (1949), Lamming's own account of the novel's background (The Guardian, 24 October 2002), and the reception by Richard Wright, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Sandra Pouchet Paquet and Joyce E. Jonas as quoted there. The article has no plot summary.

title: The Emigrants (Lamming novel) (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (1 chunk). Publication history, the University of Michigan Press description, Nicholas Robinette's chapter (2014) and the Kirkus review of 1 April 1955 as quoted there; the claim that the novel follows the protagonist of In the Castle of My Skin is cited to the British Library.

title: George Lamming (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
reliability_notes: Biography article read in full (chunk 0 of 3). One-line characterisations of each novel and of The Pleasures of Exile, and the 1992 Conversations; dates Natives of My Person 1971 against 1972 in the other sources. The AI-generated topic pages linked from it were not used.

title: George Lamming (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Gale's Contemporary Black Biography)
reliability_notes: Contemporary Black Biography entry by James M. Manheim, read in full (chunks 0-1 of 6): life, career, the San Cristobal novels, the Freedom Riders documentary script, honours and selected writings. It gives the debut novel once as 'The Castle of My Skin', lists Coming, Coming Home twice (1995 and 2001) and calls the fourth novel 'A Season of Adventure'.

title: Lamming, George (Eric) (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Contemporary Novelists)
reliability_notes: Contemporary Novelists entry on the same Encyclopedia.com page (chunks 1-3 of 6): biographical data, a full bibliography (novels with first London and New York editions, uncollected stories, other books, anthologies edited, theatrical activity) and Gerald Moore's critical essay on all six novels. The main source for the plots of Of Age and Innocence and Water with Berries.

title: Lamming, George (Encyclopedia.com, compiling the Encyclopedia of African-American Culture and History)
reliability_notes: Third entry on the same page (chunk 3 of 6, read in part): an overview of the novels as one corpus and of The Pleasures of Exile and its reading of Caliban. The author of the entry is not given in the part read.

title: In the Castle of My Skin (Encyclopedia.com, compiling Gale's Novels for Students)
reliability_notes: Novels for Students entry: introduction, author biography and the chapter-by-chapter plot summary of all fourteen chapters read in full (chunks 0-2 of 16); the start of the character list read; themes, style, historical context, criticism and Carolyn T. Brown's essay seen only in a search extract. The basis of the plot summary of In the Castle of My Skin.

title: Season of Adventure by George Lamming (EBSCO Research Starters)
reliability_notes: Consulted through a search-result extract only, not opened: the two parts of the novel, a plot outline and character notes (Fola Piggott, Charlot Pressior). The basis of the plot summary of Season of Adventure, which agrees with Gerald Moore's account and the publisher's description.

title: Natives of My Person: Analysis of Major Characters (EBSCO Research Starters)
reliability_notes: Consulted through a search-result extract only: notes on the Commandant, the Lady of the House of Trade and Justice, Sasha, the Steward, the Surgeon, the Priest, the Steward's wife, the orphan girl and Admiral Badaloza. The only source for Sasha's killing of Surgeon and Steward.

title: George Lamming Critical Essays (eNotes)
author_or_editor: eNotes (excerpting Helen Tiffin, 1979, and Avis G. McDonald, 1987)
reliability_notes: Consulted through a search-result extract only: passages on Natives of My Person from Helen Tiffin (essay of October 1979) and Avis G. McDonald (essay of 1987), the latter giving the novel's three parts. The full essays were not read.

title: Conversations: George Lamming: Essays, Addresses and Interviews, 1953-1990 (Google Books record)
reliability_notes: Consulted through a search-result extract: title, editors (Richard Drayton and Andaiye), publisher (Karia Press), year (1992), length (300 pages) and ISBN 0946918880. Only the bibliographic record; the contents were not seen.

title: George Lamming: The Vocation of Writing and his Critical Social Engagement (Anthurium)
reliability_notes: Consulted through a search-result extract only: its references cite 'Politics and Culture' (pp. 71-83) and George Kent's interview '"A Future They Must Learn"' (pp. 86-105) in Conversations (1992), and it describes Lamming's solidarity with Andaiye's political work in Guyana. The author's name was not in the extract.

title: Season of Adventure (University of Michigan Press)
reliability_notes: Publisher's description of the 1999 Ann Arbor Paperbacks edition, consulted through search-result extracts: Fola as a light-skinned middle-class girl in recently independent San Cristobal, the ceremony of the souls and the steel drums. Used only to corroborate the plot outline.

title: Commonwealth Foundation prizes (Wikipedia), sections on the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and the Commonwealth Short Story Competition
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (chunks 0-6 of 7). The tables cite the Commonwealth Foundation's list of regional winners 1987-2007 (archived PDF, not consulted). All Best Book winners 1987-2000, Best First Book winners 1989-2000 and Short Story Competition winners 1996-2000 were transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/commonwealth_writers_prize_1987_2000.csv (112 rows). Points to check: the country column gives Canada for Olive Senior (1987) and South Africa for Lindsey Collen in 2005 though Mauritius in 1994; 1996 (Best Book) and 1989 (Best First Book) have no African selection; the 1998 short-story winner's title is blank. Used for discovery only.

title: Heinemann Caribbean Writers Series (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (1 chunk). The introduction quotes Anthony van der Vlies in The Oxford Companion to the Book (2010): the series was founded in 1970, modelled on the African Writers Series, and Michael Anthony's The Year in San Fernando was its first title. The table lists only 33 titles, with years of first publication rather than of the series edition, so it is a selection, not a bibliography of the series. Transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/heinemann_caribbean_writers_series.csv (33 rows; the anthology row is credited to its editor). Errors and doubtful entries: Witchbroom (1992) is credited by the table's grouped cell to Vanessa Spence, but Wikipedia's article on Lawrence Scott (seen as a search extract) lists it as his first novel (Allison & Busby, 1992; Heinemann Caribbean Writers Series, 1993), and the CSV credits it to Scott; the table dates Paulette Ramsay's Aunt Jen 1970, but WorldCat (OCLC 51668740) and Google Books, seen as search extracts, record Oxford: Heinemann, 2002, in the Caribbean Writers Series, so the CSV gives 2002 and the title falls outside the inventory; the genre 'Novel' for Michael Anthony's Cricket in the Road comes from a grouped cell and was not checked. Used for discovery only.

title: Sam Selvon (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (2 chunks). Cites Kenneth Ramchand's ODNB entry (2004; not consulted), Louis James's obituary in The Independent (20 April 1994; not consulted) and Michel Fabre's interview in Susheila Nasta (ed.), Critical Perspectives on Sam Selvon (1988), for Selvon's account of writing The Lonely Londoners in dialect. Gives birth and death (20 May 1923, San Fernando - 16 April 1994, Piarco International Airport), the pseudonyms of his Trinidad Guardian years, the Dundee fellowship (1975-77), the move to Canada, two marriages, Guggenheim Fellowships in 1955 and 1968, and a bibliography. Discrepancies with other sources: Turn Again Tiger is dated 1958 in the text and 1959 in the list; Eldorado West One is dated 1988 in the text and 1989 in the list; the list alone includes 'A Meap Story' (1954).

title: The Lonely Londoners (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext, chunk 0 of 2 read (overview, social commentary, narrative technique and the start of the adaptations). Cites Susheila Nasta's introduction to the Penguin edition (2006), Christian Mair in The Journal of Commonwealth Literature 24.1 (1989) and Helon Habila in The Guardian (17 March 2007). First publishers: Allan Wingate (UK) and St Martin's Press (US), 1956, 142 pp.

title: Samuel Selvon: 'The Lonely Londoners' - 1956, by Bill Schwarz (London Fictions)
publisher: Five Leaves (London Fictions, ed. Andrew Whitehead and Jerry White); online at londonfictions.com
reliability_notes: Chunks 0-2 of 4 read (the essay in full; chunk 3 is site navigation). Bill Schwarz is a professor in the School of English and Drama at Queen Mary, University of London. Quotes the opening and closing passages of the novel, discusses the summer section, Galahad's soliloquy on colour and Moses' sense of stasis, and locates the novel's London (Westbourne Grove, Bayswater, the Harrow Road). States that Selvon confirmed T. S. Eliot's influence and read for the BBC's Caribbean Voices. Used for The Lonely Londoners and for Selvon's early years in London.

title: The Lonely Londoners Full Plot Summary (GradeSaver)
author_or_editor: John Melendez; edited by James Cooper
reliability_notes: Last reviewed 29 June 2023. Chunk 0 of 2 read; the remainder (Harris's party, the pigeon, the close) was seen as search-result extracts, including the guide's summary of pp. 101-129. A study guide, not scholarship: used only for the order of episodes and for details of minor characters, which agree with Wikipedia and Schwarz where they overlap. Calls Lewis Tolroy's brother; other accounts make him a brother-in-law, so the record does not state the relationship.

title: Samuel Selvon (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
reliability_notes: Biography read (the AI panel on the page was ignored). Dates Ways of Sunlight 1958 and I Hear Thunder 1962, against 1957 and 1963 in the other sources; places his death in Port of Spain, where Wikipedia has Piarco International Airport; dates his start at the Trinidad Guardian to 1946. Calls Turn Again Tiger 'perhaps his best' and notes its extensive use of dialect.

title: Samuel Selvon, by Kwame S. N. Dawes (EBSCO Research Starters)
reliability_notes: Chunks 0-1 of 3 read (biography, list of works and annotated bibliography). Lists eleven long fictions including 'A Drink of Water' (1968), not listed elsewhere, and omits 'A Meap Story'; dates the Guggenheim Fellowships 1954 and 1968 (Wikipedia: 1955 and 1968); calls his wartime post 'telegraph operator' (Wikipedia: wireless operator); lists writer-in-residence posts at Alberta, Calgary, Victoria, Winnipeg and Dundee; mentions an unfinished novel, 'A High of Zero', and an autobiography in progress at his death.

title: Sam Selvon (South Asian Britain: Connecting Histories)
author_or_editor: Making Britain / South Asian Britain project, University of Bristol and partners
reliability_notes: Chunk 0 of 2 read (biography and published works, with first publishers). Gives his parents (Bertwyn Fraser Selvon; Daisy Irene Dickson), his literary editorship of the Sunday Guardian, more than twenty BBC radio plays, the television scripts Anansi the Spider Man and Home, Sweet India, the script of Horace Ove's Pressure (1976), and his involvement with the Caribbean Artists Movement in the late 1960s. The list of published works is the record's main check for first editions: Allan Wingate (1952-1956), MacGibbon & Kee (1957-1970), Davis Poynter (1972, 1975), Longman (1983, 1989) and Peepal Tree (1988, 1991). Posthumous books outside the period: Poems of Sam Selvon (2012) and Calypso in London (2023).

title: Samuel Selvon (Asian Heritage in Canada, Toronto Metropolitan University Library)
reliability_notes: Chunk 0 of 2 read. Reprints publishers' synopses of The Housing Lark (Lynne Rienner, 1990), Moses Migrating (Lynne Rienner, 2009), Turn Again Tiger (Heinemann, 1979) and Ways of Sunlight (Longman, 1987), and records the 1984 Georges Bugnet Award (Alberta Literary Awards) for Moses Migrating. The synopsis printed under Turn Again Tiger describes A Brighter Sun, of which it calls the later novel a sequel.

title: Eldorado West One (Peepal Tree Press)
reliability_notes: Read in full. Seven one-act plays bringing to the stage characters from The Lonely Londoners and Moses Ascending, edited with an introduction and notes by Susheila Nasta; quotes Louis James in Wasafiri. ISBN 9780948833069, 156 pp. The page's publication date, 6 January 1998, is presumably that of a later printing; the other sources give 1988.

title: Highway in the Sun (Peepal Tree Press)
reliability_notes: Read in full. Names and describes the four plays (Highway in the Sun, Home Sweet India, Turn Again Tiger, Harvest in Wilderness), says they were first broadcast by the BBC in the 1970s, and gives the publication date 1 December 1991 (ISBN 9780948833076, 215 pp.). The author profile on the same page describes Selvon's family and his years as a wireless operator.

title: Sam Selvon at 100 (1923-2023), by Shireen Ali (Caribbean Beat)
publisher: Caribbean Beat (issue 179, November/December 2023), in partnership with the Bocas Lit Fest
reliability_notes: The first chunk of the page (8 chunks) contained only captions; the descriptions of Turn Again Tiger, I Hear Thunder, The Housing Lark and Those Who Eat the Cascadura were seen as search-result extracts. Dates Turn Again Tiger 1959. Journalism, used for one-line accounts of plots and corroborated where possible.

title: Race and Community in Sam Selvon's Fiction (Northern Arizona University web essay)
reliability_notes: Seen only as search-result extracts; the author is not named in them. Discusses Turn Again Tiger, I Hear Thunder, The Housing Lark and Those Who Eat the Cascadura and quotes the novels with page references. Used only to corroborate details given by another source.

title: A Brighter Sun Summary (eNotes)
reliability_notes: Seen only as search-result extracts (the summary and the analysis pages). Used for the course of the plot of A Brighter Sun, which no other source consulted narrates; the record is marked partially verified for that reason.

title: Journal of West Indian Literature 24.2 (November 2016), Caribbean Ecocriticism special issue
reliability_notes: Seen only as a search-result extract from one essay on The Plains of Caroni, whose author is not named in the extract. It cites Michel Fabre for Tate and Lyle's sponsorship of Selvon's 1969 return to Trinidad, quotes the novel (MacGibbon & Kee, 1970) with page references, and describes Romesh, the harvester trial, Teeka and Balgobin.

title: The Novel since 1970 (ResearchGate PDF)
reliability_notes: Seen only as a search-result extract; the author and the volume are not named in it. Summarises The Plains of Caroni (Balgobin, Seeta, Romesh, the mechanical harvester) and cites a 1995 study, 'Selvon and the Limits of Heroism: A Reading of The Plains of Caroni'. Agrees in every detail with the Journal of West Indian Literature essay.

title: Moses Ascending (Penguin Modern Classics description, as reproduced by booksellers)
publisher: Penguin Modern Classics (ISBN 9780241504390); reproduced by New Beacon Books, Shakespeare and Company and an AbeBooks listing of the 1975 first edition
reliability_notes: Seen only as search-result extracts, in several identical copies. A publisher's blurb, used for the premise and the episodes it names; the AbeBooks listing of the first edition (London, 1975, ISBN 0706701887) spells the publisher 'David-Poynter', where South Asian Britain has Davis Poynter, and adds that Moses shelters Pakistani immigrants.

title: An Island Is a World (Mawenzi House)
reliability_notes: Seen only as a search-result extract. The publisher's description of its 2019 edition (ISBN 978-1-77415-004-7, 304 pp.), quoting The Globe and Mail.

title: Of Selvon and Sentimentality: Diasporic Rememberings (Anthurium)
source_type: scholarly journal article (introduction to a special issue)
reliability_notes: Seen only as a search-result extract. Introduces a special issue arising from the 'Samuel Selvon @100' panel (Canadian Association for Postcolonial Studies, 2023); notes Ramabai Espinet's case for reconsidering An Island Is a World, Kris Singh's essay on cane in 'Cane is Bitter' and The Plains of Caroni, and Nalini Mohabir's account of Selvon's thoughts on return, including the BBC play Home Sweet India (1970).

title: List of Sahitya Akademi Award winners for English (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read (chunk 0 of 2, which holds the whole table from 1960 to 2011). The infobox cites the Sahitya Akademi's own award list (not consulted). All 30 awards of 1960-2000 were transcribed with the table's book category into research/installment_10/lists/sahitya_akademi_award_english_1960_2000.csv. The table has no entry for 1961-1963, 1966, 1968, 1970, 1972-1974, 1995 and 1997; whether no award was made in those years is not stated, so no rows were invented for them. Years are award years: a book can be several years older (The Guide is of 1958). Several winners are biographers or scholars (Verrier Elwin, Niharranjan Ray, Nirad C. Chaudhuri, Sarvepalli Gopal, K. R. Srinivasa Iyengar, G. N. Devy). Used for discovery only.

title: Governor General's Award for English-language fiction (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read for 1936-2009 (chunks 0-4 of 8); each row cites a contemporary newspaper report. Every winner of 1946-2000 and every finalist of 1979-2000 (the article says advance shortlists began in 1979 and were omitted only for 1981) was transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/governor_generals_award_english_fiction_1946_2000.csv (129 rows; no award in 1965 and 1967; two winners in 1968). The table does not mark translations. Five winners are English translations and are not used as evidence: Gabrielle Roy's The Tin Flute (1947) and Street of Riches (1957), from French (a LibraryThing author note, seen as a search extract); Germaine Guevremont's The Outlander (1950), from French, translated by Eric Sutton (Wikipedia's article on the novel, seen as a search extract); Igor Gouzenko's The Fall of a Titan (1954), from Russian, and Josef Skvorecky's The Engineer of Human Souls (1984), from Czech, both from general reference knowledge and not checked against a source in this pass. The 1952-1953 winner, whom the table calls David Walker, is recorded as David Harry Walker, the fuller form of his Library of Congress heading (LCCN n50020271, in the Post45 HathiTrust fiction metadata), because the bare name folds to the abolitionist David Walker (d. 1830) in the master database. Used for discovery only.

title: Miles Franklin Award (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read for 1957-2009 (chunks 0-2 of 13); most rows cite contemporary reports in The Canberra Times, The Age or The Sydney Morning Herald. All winners of 1957-2000 were transcribed with their publishers into research/installment_10/lists/miles_franklin_award_1957_2000.csv (45 rows: the award was withheld in 1973 and 1983; joint winners in 1962 and 2000). The article explains that the prize was dated by the year of publication to 1987 and by the year of the award from 1989, so there is no prize called 1988 although the series is unbroken; the CSV keeps the article's years. The 1995 winner is recorded as Helen Darville, the name the table links to; the book was published under the name Helen Demidenko. The shortlists in the later part of the article were not transcribed. Used for discovery only.

title: Pulitzer Prize for Drama (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read for 1917-2015 (chunks 0 and 2-7 of 10). The article's notes on each year's jury cite Heinz-Dietrich Fischer and Erika J. Fischer, The Pulitzer Prize Archive: Chronicle of the Pulitzer Prizes for Drama (K. G. Saur, 2008), which was not consulted. Transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/pulitzer_prize_drama_1946_2000.csv (178 rows): every result of 1946-2000 (no award in 1947, 1951, 1963, 1964, 1966, 1968, 1972, 1974, 1986 and 1997), the finalists the table gives from 1983, and the plays the notes say a jury shortlisted, recommended, considered or commended (role jury_shortlist, with the note's wording). The table lists all credited names of a musical without their roles; the CSV assigns book, lyric, composer and director roles from general reference knowledge, and composers (Richard Rodgers, Jerry Bock, Marvin Hamlisch, Bob Telson) and Michael Bennett, who conceived, directed and choreographed A Chorus Line, are not used as evidence. Gian Carlo Menotti's opera The Consul, which the 1950 jury recommended, was not transcribed. Used for discovery only.

title: King's Gold Medal for Poetry (Wikipedia; formerly Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (1 chunk); the article carries a 'more citations needed' banner and gives recipients by year without titles. It says the medal was open only to British subjects living in the United Kingdom until 1985, when it was extended to the other Commonwealth realms. The 30 recipients of 1952-2000 (there is no entry between 1940 and 1952) were transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/queens_gold_medal_poetry_1952_2000.csv. Sorley MacLean (1990) wrote in Scottish Gaelic and is given priority 2; Arthur Waley (1953) is known as a translator of Chinese and Japanese literature. Used for discovery only.

title: Evening Standard Theatre Award for Best Play (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read for the 1st-56th ceremonies (chunks 0-1 of 4). The table numbers ceremonies rather than giving years; the article says the award has been presented since 1955, and its dated citations for the 47th-56th ceremonies (2001-2010) agree with year = 1954 + ceremony number, which the CSV uses. All winners of the 1st-46th ceremonies (1955-2000) were transcribed into research/installment_10/lists/evening_standard_award_best_play_1955_2000.csv (54 rows; two winners at the 11th; N/A at the 45th, 1999). For plays in translation the table names the original author and the translator (Anouilh and Lucienne Hill, 1961 and 1963; Brecht and Eric Bentley, 1962, without roles; De Filippo, and Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall, 1973; Joshua Sobol and David Lan, 1989): original authors are not used as evidence and translators are priority 3. The table names only Christopher Fry for Tiger at the Gates (1955), his English version of Giraudoux's La guerre de Troie n'aura pas lieu (from general reference knowledge), so Fry is recorded as its translator. Used for discovery only.

title: Gabriel Okara (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (2 chunks). Gives birth on 24 April 1921 at Bomoundi and death on 25 March 2019 at Yenagoa; the 1953 Nigerian Festival of Arts award for 'The Call of the River Nun'; Northwestern University in 1949; the 1962 Makerere conference; Biafran roving ambassador with Achebe in 1969; director of the Rivers State Publishing House 1972-1980 (citing Britannica); the 1979 Commonwealth Poetry Prize for The Fisherman's Invocation; and a selected bibliography that dates Little Snake and Little Frog 1981 and An Adventure to Juju Island 1992. Quotes Britannica on The Voice and Brenda Marie Osbey's introduction to the Collected Poems (2016). Several statements rest on Nigerian newspaper obituaries, which were not consulted.

title: The Voice (novel) (Wikipedia)
reliability_notes: Raw wikitext read in full (1 chunk). A short article: a two-sentence plot that sets the novel in post-independence Igboland (doubtful: the other sources consulted connect the novel's language with Ijo, Okara's own people, and give no setting); Britannica's description of the Ijo-patterned English; Thomas Hinde's review in the Times Literary Supplement; references to studies by Patrick Scott (1990), Edwin Thumboo (2007) and Luke Eyoh (2012), none consulted. The infobox gives Africana as publisher with the 1964 date, 127 pages and ISBN 0-8419-0015-9, mixing the first and the 1970 American editions.

title: Okara, Gabriel 1921-, by James M. Manheim (Contemporary Black Biography, via Encyclopedia.com)
publisher: Gale (Contemporary Black Biography), reproduced by Encyclopedia.com
reliability_notes: Read in full (chunks 0-1 of 3; the third is site navigation). Cites Contemporary Authors Online (2001), DLB 125, Modern Black Writers (2000) and other Gale references. Gives birth on 24 (or 21) April 1921; Government College, Umuahia, 1935-1941; the Government Press 1945-1954; 'The Call of the River Nun' written 1950, prized 1953 and published in Black Orpheus in 1957, and called his first published poem; a Northwestern journalism degree in 1960; 'The Snowflakes Sail Gently Down' written in Illinois; the plot and language of The Voice, with Okara's statement of why he wrote it and the opposed judgments of Wole Soyinka and Emmanuel Obiechina; a 1969 visit to the United States for Biafra; the 1978 collection, whose title poem it says won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize ('Commonwealth Joint Poetry Award, 1979' in its summary); and children's works of the 1990s based on folktales. Lists The Voice as published by F. Watts, 1964. The publication year 2002 is inferred from its sources and was not stated.

title: Okara, Gabriel (Imomotimi Gbaingbain), by Howard Sergeant (Contemporary Poets, via Encyclopedia.com)
publisher: St. James Press (Contemporary Poets), reproduced by Encyclopedia.com
reliability_notes: Read in full (chunk 0 of 2; the second is site navigation).
